title: Your Child Can Pass a Math Test and Still Not Understand Math
author: Quest Schooling
summary: A homeschooling parent reflects on the failure mode of worksheet-centric math education: children who ace fraction tests but cannot apply fractions in real-life cooking. The author traces this to the 'orphaned tool' problem — concepts practiced in complete isolation from the real-world problems that originally motivated their invention. The article proposes a Three Loops of Learning framework: understand why the tool was invented, practice using it, then use it to solve a problem that matters. Every human discipline was invented to solve a recurring problem — fractions exist not to fill workbooks but to divide resources. The shift from workbooks to purpose-driven learning transformed the author's children from disengaged to energized, from performing for scores to building things they are genuinely proud of.
points: Children who ace fraction worksheets can freeze when asked to triple a recipe in a real kitchen — test performance and genuine capability are not the same thing.
The deepest flaw in traditional schooling is the 'orphaned tool' — a concept practiced in isolation and never reconnected to the real-world problem that motivated its invention.
Every human discipline was invented to solve a recurring problem; starting with that problem, rather than the mechanics, motivates children to learn the tool.
The Three Loops of Learning: understand why the tool was invented, practice using it, then use it to solve a problem that matters to someone.
The proof of learning isn't a grade on a scorecard — it is several loaves of freshly baked bread and a kid who feels genuinely proud of their skillset.
quotes: I had quietly begun confusing performance on paper with genuine capability.
